query: Starting from an as-processed Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy with a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution-plus-intermetallic state and a target density below 6 g/cm3, what single intervention could overcome performance limitations associated with stable intermetallic formation while improving room-temperature compressive behavior, corrosion resistance, and resistance to high-temperature oxidation? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts measurable changes relative to the as-processed baseline, defines the relevant composition, temperature, exposure-time, and test-environment boundaries, cites supporting evidence from previously reported Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys, and proposes a controlled experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The introduction of a Mo addition to a Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy can overcome performance limitations associated with stable intermetallic formation while improving room-temperature compressive behavior, corrosion resistance, and resistance to high-temperature oxidation.
generation.material_initial_state: As-processed Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy with a non-equilibrium, metastable solid-solution-plus-intermetallic state
generation.conditions: Target density below 6 g/cm3, room temperature, and high-temperature oxidation environment
generation.structural_mediator: Passive film structure and Cr2O3 formation
generation.mechanism: Mo-induced optimization of the passive film structure and enhanced Cr2O3 formation
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved room-temperature compressive behavior, corrosion resistance, and resistance to high-temperature oxidation
generation.baseline: As-processed Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy without Mo addition
generation.boundary: Temperature range from room temperature to 1000 °C, exposure time up to 100 h, and test environment including 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution and high-temperature oxidation
generation.uncertainty: The exact amount of Mo addition required to achieve optimal performance and the potential effects of other alloying elements on the properties of the Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy

falsification_experiment.design: Controlled experiment with varying Mo additions to Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys, tested under room temperature and high-temperature oxidation conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the introduction of Mo addition does not result in improved room-temperature compressive behavior, corrosion resistance, and resistance to high-temperature oxidation, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) have attracted extensive attention since 2004 for their excellent properties [,]. Due to the high configuration entropy, the alloy tends to form simple solid solution phases instead of intermetallic compounds, such as BCC, FCC, and HCP [,]. In addition, the alloys are composed of multi-principal-component elements, and each component can be regulated in a wide range of atomic percentages. A vast realm of alloy composition regulation makes it possible to achieve comprehensive mechanical properties, such as high hardness and strength [,], great oxidation resistance [,], and excellent wear and corrosion resistance [,], which are in great demand for the industry as loading-bearing structures.

This study provides new perspectives and a new understanding of the oxidation and corrosion behaviors of high-entropy alloys, revealing their outstanding performance during the oxidation process. With the development of materials science, high-entropy alloys, as a novel material, possess great potential in industrial applications due to their superior mechanical properties, high-temperature resistance, and corrosion resistance. In the future, with continuous research, it is expected that high-entropy alloys will be widely applied in various fields such as aerospace, energy, chemical engineering, and automotive manufacturing. Especially in high-temperature, high-pressure, and extreme environments, they are expected to become important structural and functional materials.

Complex concentrated alloys (CCA) represent a new group of materials, with complex microstructures, comprising of a large number of elements []. CCAs extend the established limits of the high entropy alloys (HEAs) concept by allowing a smaller number of elements in the composition and in various proportions, that can deliver mixed structures containing solid solution and well dispersed intermetallic phases. CCAs generally have higher configurational entropy than conventional alloys and are capable of obtaining complex, disordered compositionally complex solid solution structures. CCAs are distinct from conventional alloys in that they are not based on a single major element and rather include several main elements, which allow a high degree of freedom in alloy compositions and properties. Their properties, such as high temperature resistance, corrosion resistance, workability, and low density, offer a remarkable advantage in the use of CCAs for various extreme conditions applications [,]. In this study, bulk samples of a CrMoNbWV high-entropy alloy (HEA) were obtained for the first time by spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed (MA) powders at 1200 °C, 1300 °C, and 1400 °C. Microstructure evolution, phase formation as well as wear and corrosion behavior were investigated. The MA powders’ phase composition was found to be represented by body-centered-cubic (BCC) solid solution. The solid solution partially decomposed to Laves phases under the sintering, such as Cr2Nb and (Fe, Cr)Nb, and NbVO4-VO oxides mixture. The temperature increase to 1400 °C led to a grain coarsening of the BCC phase and decreased the Laves phase content accompanied by precipitation at the grain boundaries. The sintered samples showed high hardness and compressive strength (2700–2800 MPa) at room temperature. The wear tests demonstrated excellent results in comparison to conventional wear-resistant composites. The obtained samples also exhibited high corrosion resistance under electrochemical tests in H2SO4 solution.
